identity.title: Learning long range dependencies through time reversal symmetry breaking

problem.claim: Develop learning algorithms for physics-grounded recurrent systems that respect physical principles and support efficient simulation and design.

contributions.claim: Proposes Recurrent Hamiltonian Echo Learning (RHEL), which authors state computes loss gradients as finite differences of trajectories in non-dissipative Hamiltonian systems.
Introduces continuous- and discrete-time formulations, with reported equivalence to the continuous adjoint method and, for Hamiltonian Recurrent Units, to BPTT.
Extends the construction to hierarchical Hamiltonian SSMs and applies it to linear and nonlinear sequence models.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish RHEL through its physical-trajectory finite-difference gradient computation and its potential implementation in non-digital physical systems.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that RHEL requires three forward passes regardless of model size, without explicit Jacobian computation or gradient-estimation variance.
The authors report training HSSMs on mid- to long-range time-series classification and regression tasks with sequence lengths reaching approximately 50,000.
Across the reported models and tasks, the authors state that RHEL consistently matches BPTT performance.

narrative_sequence.summary: Physics-grounded SSMs motivate algorithms that follow physical principles while enabling efficient simulation and design.
RHEL is introduced as a finite-difference gradient method based on Hamiltonian trajectories, with a stated three-forward-pass property.
The continuous-time method is presented with a reported formal equivalence to the continuous adjoint state method.
A discrete-time version is proposed, linked to BPTT for HRUs and generalized to hierarchical HSSMs.
HSSMs are trained on time-series tasks up to roughly 50k sequence length, with reported performance matching BPTT.

source_observation.claim: The abstract pairs a computational claim about gradient estimation with explicit equivalence statements and a comparison against BPTT across task types and sequence lengths.

lessons.interpretation: This alignment makes the method’s intended computational advantage, theoretical relationship, and empirical comparison inspectable as separate claims.
lessons.application: When presenting a new training algorithm, state its resource property, identify the regime where it corresponds to a known method, and report comparisons across the claimed operating range.
lessons.exception: This structure is unsuitable when no meaningful baseline, formal correspondence, or varied evaluation regime exists.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the conditions or proof details behind the gradient and equivalence claims.
It does not quantify the number of models, tasks, baselines, or the meaning of “consistently matches” BPTT.
Energy efficiency and physical-system implementation are presented as potential directions, not demonstrated results.

editorial_revisions.before: The authors report training HSSMs on mid- to long-range time-series classification and regression tasks with sequence lengths of approximately 50,000.
editorial_revisions.after: The authors report training HSSMs on mid- to long-range time-series classification and regression tasks with sequence lengths reaching approximately 50,000.
